title: Eggy Bread
subtitle: Thick bread soaked in beaten egg and fried in butter
excerpt: White bread soaked in beaten egg and fried in butter until golden and slightly crisp on the outside, soft and custardy inside. The British version of French toast, served sweet or savoury.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. Pain perdu listed as an English recipe under French names from at least the fourteenth century. The British name 'eggy bread' or 'poor knights of Windsor' refers to this dish. 'Poor knights of Windsor' is documented from the fourteenth century as a frugal dish for using stale bread soaked in wine or egg.

content.text: Eggy bread is the British name for what the French call pain perdu: bread soaked in beaten egg and fried in butter. The British version is usually unseasoned or lightly salted, served with ketchup or brown sauce at breakfast, or with jam or golden syrup for something sweeter. It is the most forgiving recipe imaginable: stale bread works better than fresh, and the technique is straightforward.

items.prepNote: thick slices, ideally 1 to 2 days old

content.text: Beat {{eggs}} eggs with {{whole-milk}} of milk and {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt in a shallow bowl wide enough to fit a slice of bread.
Soak {{bread-white}} slices of bread in the egg mixture, one at a time, for 20 to 30 seconds per side. The bread should absorb the egg without falling apart.
Heat {{unsalted-butter}} of butter and {{sunflower-oil}} of oil in a frying pan over medium heat until the butter foams. Wait for the foam to start to settle.
Cook the soaked bread for 2 to 3 minutes per side until deep golden. Do not rush: medium heat colours the outside without scorching it.
Serve immediately, plain, with ketchup for a savoury version, or with jam and a dusting of icing sugar for a sweeter one.

rows.cause: Bread too fresh or soaked too long
rows.fix: Use bread that is 1 to 2 days old. Soak just long enough to absorb the egg, not so long the structure breaks down.

rows.symptom: Eggy bread tastes rubbery and dry
rows.cause: Overcooked, or not enough egg in the soak
rows.fix: Use 1 egg per 2 slices and include enough milk to make a loose custard. Remove from the pan while still just set in the middle.

rows.symptom: Outside is dark before the inside is set
rows.fix: Use medium heat. Eggy bread needs time for the egg inside the bread to set without burning the outside.

rows.cause: Heat too high or no oil added
rows.fix: Add a small amount of oil to raise the smoke point of the butter, and keep the heat at medium.

content.text: Eggy bread in Britain sits between a breakfast dish and a childhood comfort food. It has been eaten in various forms since the medieval period. An old recipe called poor knights of Windsor describes bread soaked in egg and wine, then fried and served as a dessert. The modern British version is plainer than French pain perdu or American French toast. It is almost always served with something savoury: bacon, sausages, or tomato sauce.
